newsitem.title: USA: Voisey's Bay clouds rival nickel projects - miner.
newsitem.headline: Voisey's Bay clouds rival nickel projects - miner.

text.p: Nickel projects unable to start-up before the huge Voisey's Bay comes on stream, may never enjoy earnings that current high nickel prices offer, Falconbridge Limited told a recent conference.
The Canadian nickel miner also warned that new nickel projects should avoid depending on high cobalt prices to boost bottom lines.

"Many of the new projects are looking to strong positive contributions from cobalt. This could prove dangerous in the long run," Joseph Laezza, Falconbridge's vice president, sales and marketing told a recent Ryan's Notes conference.
Many of the new nickel projects will produce cobalt as a by-product. There is no incentive to slow production in the face of low cobalt prices.
"It is quite conceivable that cobalt prices could rival those of nickel during the period of lower prices at the start of the next century," Laezza said.
He forecast a long-term nickel price of $3.75 per pound over the period 1996 to 2010.
LME cash nickel settled at $3.28 per pound Monday.
The low-cost Voisey's Bay project will have a direct and quick impact on the industry by lowering its cost structure.
Laezza expected Voisey's Bay to enter full production of 122,000 tonnes of nickel from the year 2000 at the earliest.
Meanwhile demand for nickel in the key stainless steel sector was set to continue growing, Laezza said.

"The past 15 years has seen a growth of 5.3 percent in Western world stainless steel production and consequent demand. We can see no reason why the next 15 years should not see at least the same growth," Laezza said.

Over the next 15 years, nickel demand in the Western world is set to grow 3.5 percent, and by 8.5 percent in the non-Western world, giving a "conservative" average growth rate of 4.1 percent for the period up to 2010.
"Bringing the supply and demand projections together, we find that we are likely to see a nickel market continuing to be in deficit through to and including 1999," Laezza said.
After 2000 Laezza forecast about five years of market surpluses.
